The Blacktail redhorse Moxostoma poecilurum is a freshwater catostomid native to Gulf Coast drainages of the southeastern United States. Recent field surveys conducted in Alabama and Mississippi indicate that females reach sexual maturation at a total length of 34 cm [Lp = 34 cm], a relatively modest size that reflects the attainment of puberty within three to four years post-hatching. Growth curves fitted to mark-recapture data show that the ultimate total length for this species is 51 cm [Li = 51 cm], placing it as a medium-sized member of the genus Moxostoma. The maximum adult wet weight derived from this length-mass relationship reaches 1,260 grams [Wwi = 1,260 grams], a value consistent with the robust body form typical of benthic-feeding suckers. In contrast, newly emerged prolarvae are extremely small; the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0098 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0098 grams], reflecting the modest yolk reserves contained within the demersal, adhesive eggs. This nearly six orders-of-magnitude increase in body mass from the yolk-sac larva to the fully grown adult underscores a substantial capacity for somatic growth over the species' life span.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum longevity documented for Moxostoma poecilurum is 8 years [am = 8 years], a duration that is typical for catostomids of comparable body size. The maximum reproductive rate observed at this same temperature reflects a combination of clutch size and spawning frequency. Individual females produce up to 1,260 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = up to 1,260 eggs per spawning event], and they undergo roughly 12 spawning events per year [F_R_i = roughly 12 spawning events per year], resulting in a high annual fecundity that supports population persistence in stable stream environments. This iteroparous strategy, with multiple clutches distributed across the warmer months, buffers against sporadic recruitment failures common in lotic habitats subject to seasonal flooding.

The pronounced disparity in wet weight between the earliest life stages and the fully grown adult is well illustrated by comparing the mass of the recently emerged yolk-sac larva with that of the mature fish. Field-caught gravid females, for instance, yield eggs that individually weigh roughly 9.8 milligrams [Wwb = roughly 9.8 milligrams] at the moment of oviposition, a value that aligns well with data from other medium-bodied Moxostoma species studied in the same region. Once the free-swimming larva transitions to active feeding on benthic microinvertebrates, growth proceeds rapidly during the first summer, and by the end of the first year, juveniles commonly attain a total length of 8 to 12 cm. The allometric relationship used to estimate ultimate body mass from length indicates that a fish reaching the asymptotic length of 51 cm [Li = 51 cm] will have an estimated wet weight of 1.26 kilograms [Wwi = 1.26 kilograms], a value that has been confirmed by direct weighing of large adults in several Gulf Coast populations.

Sexual maturation in female Blacktail redhorse is tied more closely to body size than to chronological age, although the two are obviously correlated under typical growing conditions. Based on size-at-age keys developed from otolith annuli, females attain a total length of 34 cm [Lp = 34 cm] between their third and fourth year of life, marking the onset of reproductive maturity. This length at puberty is consistent across most sampled drainages, though slight regional differences have been noted in slower-growing populations from headwater streams. The size threshold itself likely reflects the attainment of sufficient body cavity volume to accommodate developing oocytes, as well as the accumulation of lipid reserves necessary to sustain vitellogenesis. Once pubertal size is reached, females begin participating in spawning aggregations that form over gravel riffles during spring and early summer, with individual reproductive output increasing in subsequent years as body size continues to increase incrementally toward the ultimate total length of 51 cm [Li = 51 cm].

The trade-off between current reproduction and future survival in this iteroparous species is mediated by the thermal regime of the stream environment. In laboratory trials conducted at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the combined maximum reproductive rate described earlier yields a daily fecundity that, when integrated over the active spawning season, approaches the upper physiological limit for a fish of this size. Field evidence suggests that older, larger females contribute disproportionately to cohort recruitment, as their larger body size allows for greater clutch volumes and extended spawning seasons. The demographic consequences of this reproductive skew are important for population management, particularly in regulated river systems where thermal cues for spawning may be altered by hypolimnetic dam releases. Conservation efforts for Moxostoma poecilurum therefore require maintaining thermal regimes that support spawning activity and juvenile growth throughout the warmer months.
